Deciding on which Model

Classification:

Regression:

Confusion Matrices

A confusion matrix helps assess a classification model's performance by tabulating each of the four possible outcomes from a binary prediction task

  refer to data points belonging to the target class (win), while   refer to data points belonging to the non-target class (loss)

Model Evaluation · Confusion Matrices07

Type 1 vs. Type 2 Errors

Type 2 errors are called "false negatives"

Type 1 errors are called "false positives"

Depending on the task at hand, we may care more about these types of errors, but only considering the overall accuracy may hide them from us.

Model Evaluation · Confusion Matrices08

Type 1 vs. Type 2 Errors

Consider a task in which we're performing a cancer screening, with the presence of cancer being the positive class.

If we have a dataset with 998 healthy examples, and 2 cancerous examples, we could get an overall accuracy of 99.8% by just predicting that everyone is healthy!

However, missing the 2 sick patients would be false negatives, and if we're trying to catch deadly diseases, making these type 2 errors are extremely costly!

Model Evaluation · Confusion Matrices10

Type 1 and Type 2 Errors in the Body

Our immune system is a classifier: every cell and molecule it meets is either "self" or "not self".

  • False positive: attacking our own cells, which is what happens in autoimmune diseases like type 1 diabetes
  • False negative:   a virus or bacterium, and getting sick

The body can't push both to zero, so it trades one against the other, the same as moving a decision threshold. ROC curves started out with radar operators, and Green and Swets (1966) brought them into psychology to measure how well people hear faint tones.

Model Evaluation · Confusion Matrices12

K-Fold Cross-Validation

The best way to get an accurate accuracy is to use a method called K-Fold Cross-Validation

In K-Fold Cross-Validation, we split our dataset into K folds, with one of the folds acting as the testing data, and the remaining folds serving as the training data.

We can then report the average accuracy across all K results.

Model Evaluation · Grid Search13

Accuracy and K-Fold in sklearn

Like usual, it's very easy to run K-fold cross-validation and produce a confusion matrix in sklearn

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_predict
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix
games = pd.read_csv("nd_football.csv")
X = games[["nd_total_yards", "opp_total_yards"]] / 100
y = 1 - games["win"] # a loss is our positive class
model = LogisticRegression(C=1e9)
pred = cross_val_predict(model, X, y, cv=5)
print(confusion_matrix(y, pred, labels=[1, 0]))
Output
[[19 16]
 [ 7 99]]

Model Evaluation · Grid Search17

Precision vs. Recall

Precision only looks inside the circle, where 19 of the 26 games are losses. Recall only looks at the left half, where 19 of the 35 losses made it into the circle.

Model Evaluation · Grid Search18

Precision vs. Recall

Notice what happens if the circle gets bigger. It picks up more of the missed losses, so recall goes up, but it also picks up more wins, so precision goes down. Shrink it and the opposite happens. Usually we can trade one for the other

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_predict
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report
games = pd.read_csv("nd_football.csv")
X = games[["nd_total_yards", "opp_total_yards"]] / 100
y = 1 - games["win"] # a loss is our positive class
model = LogisticRegression(C=1e9)
pred = cross_val_predict(model, X, y, cv=5)
print(classification_report(y, pred, digits=3,
target_names=["win", "loss"]))

Model Evaluation · Grid Search21

Accuracy vs. Precision vs. Recall

  • Accuracy - when class distribution is balanced and false positives and false negatives have similar consequences.
  • Precision - when false positives are costly or undesirable
  • Recall - when false negatives are more critical than false positives
  • F1 - when you need a balance between precision and recall and the class distribution is imbalanced.
Model Evaluation · Grid Search22

Evaluating Decision Thresholds

Another parameter that we could change is where the decision threshold lies, thus far for logistic regression we've just set it to 0.5

Every threshold gives a different confusion matrix, and raising recall costs precision.

Rather than pick one threshold, we can plot all of them. This is a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. From this we can get a single number called the AUC (Area Under Curve)

Model Evaluation · Grid Search23

Evaluating Regression Tasks

Remember that for regression tasks we are trying to predict  

Because regression tasks are supervised, we have ground-truth so we can tell how far away our predicted answers are from the ground truth.

These gaps are called the   (R) and the goal of regression is to minimize the residuals.

Model Evaluation · Assessing Regression24

Residuals Plot

A residual plot is a graph that shows the residuals on the vertical axis and the independent variable on the horizontal axis.

If the points in a residual plot are randomly dispersed around the horizontal axis, a linear regression model is appropriate for the data, otherwise, a non-linear model is more appropriate.

Model Evaluation · Assessing Regression25

Regression Tasks - R²

R² indicates the proportion of variance in the dependent variable that can be explained by the independent variable(s) in a model.

R^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum_i (y_i - \yhat_i)^2}{\sum_i (y_i - \bar{y})^2}

R² shows how well the regression line fits the data, with a value ranging from 0 (poor fit) to 1 (perfect fit).

Model Evaluation · Assessing Regression26

Mean Squared Error

Another option is, using the residuals, we can write a number of different error functions for regression tasks:

  • Residual Sum of Squares (RSS)
  • Mean Absolute Error (MAE)
  •   (MSE)
  • Mean Percentage Error (MPE)
  • Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE)
  • Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE)

MSE measures the average squared difference between the estimated values and the actual value

\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \yhat_i)^2

Assessing Clustering

Assessing unsupervised learning is difficult as there are no   against which we can compare results.

We often don't know what the right answer is!

Model Evaluation · Assessing Unsupervised Methods29

Silhouette Score

Silhouette score is a numerical value that measures how well a data point belongs to its cluster and how separated it is from other clusters.

The score ranges from -1 to 1, with higher values indicating better clustering.

Model Evaluation · Assessing Unsupervised Methods30

Dendrograms

A dendrogram is a branching diagram that shows the relationships between classes

To assess a clustering, cut the tree where the vertical lines are longest. Here the last merge (1.15) is far above the one before it (0.66), so two clusters is the natural cut.

Model Evaluation · Assessing Unsupervised Methods31

Elbow Plots

Previously, we have used elbow plots to estimate the number of   to use on a data set.

In cluster analysis, we can plot the sum of squared distances from each point to its centroid as a function of the number of clusters and pick the elbow of the curve as the number of clusters to use.
